[EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]

Th e first quarterly National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2025/26 covers the period from 1st July to 30th September 2025. Th e report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports to Parliament for the National and County governments.

Th e National Government's gross budget for FY 2025/26 is Kshs.4.69 trillion, compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion for FY 2024/25. Th e gross budget comprises Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which accounts for 16 per cent of the gross national budget and 29 per cent of the annual gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised the ministerial recurrent allocation of Kshs.1.80 trillion (38 per cent of the gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.14 trillion (46 per cent of the annual gross national budget).

Development expenditure with the highest spending included Capital Transfers by the MDAs in subsidies, grants, or direct transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) at Kshs.80.76 billion, representing 61 per cent of the gross development spending. Other major development expenditures included Construction and Civil Works at Kshs.32.56 billion and the Construction of Non-residential Buildings at Kshs.8.27 billion, representing 25 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively, of the gross development expenditure.

A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.164.04 billion was spent on Compensation to Employees, representing 38 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs and 28 per cent of the revenue collected, which is in line with the requirement in PFM Regulations 26(1) of 2015 that ministerial expenditure should not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally. Total Current transfers to other government institutions were Kshs.171.68 billion and subsidies Kshs.16.44 billion, representing 40 per cent and 4 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure, respectively. Other expenses Implementation Status were Kshs.4.96 billion for travel, Kshs.9.20 billion for security operations and Kshs.5.90 billion for school examination invigilation.

In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed to ensure seamless budget implementation not only in the current financial year but also for posterity. Th ese

included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes and Public debt management.

Th is will ensure transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources, as well as the timely implementation of planned activities.

To enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns. Recurrent expenditure should be contained through expenditure rationalisation, efficiency gains, and stronger public financial management controls.

text:
[1.  INTRODUCTION]

Th is report was prepared in fulfilment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments.

Th is report is in line with Section 9(2) of the Controller of Budget Act Cap 429, which outlines the information to be reported by the Controller of Budget in the quarterly budget implementation reports. To meet the legal requirements governing the content of budget implementation review reports, this report is organised into six chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two presents the performance of receipts into the Consolidated Fund and Exchequer Issues to Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Consolidated Fund Services and the County Revenue Fund as part of the equitable share of revenue to the forty-seven counties. Exchequer issues performance is expressed as a percentage of the annual net estimates.

Chapter Th ree presents the overall budget performance of the national government, including performance under the CFS, MDAs' expenditure by economic classification, and the stock of Trade Payables (pending bills) for national government entities.   Chapter Four presents the budget performance of the eighty-seven MDAs clustered into ten Sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, which is planned to support fiscal analysis by breaking down government fiscal statistics for comparability. It presents the approved budget referred to as the gross estimates, actual expenditure, which is further disaggregated into programme and sub-programmes performance and project implementation status for MDAs. Th e absorption rate, which measures the performance, is calculated as a proportion of actual expenditure relative to the annual budget.

text:
[2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund]

Th e Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose, or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all money collected by national government entities as a fee for services offered must be deposited into the e-citizen account, Paybill number 222222.

To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted to raise funds from various revenue sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.63 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.127.65 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.10 trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.561.81 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.

[2.4.  Exchequer Issues by Sector.]

MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the Classification of Functions of Government (COFOG), which is designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability across sectors.

Th e ten sectors are (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development, (ii) Education (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (v)

General Economic and Commercial Affairs (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations and (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation.

In the first three months of FY 2025/2026, exchequer issues to MDAs amounted to Kshs.409.80 billion, representing 22 per cent of the original annual net estimates of Kshs.1.88 trillion compared to 21 per cent (Kshs.348.63 billion), recorded in a similar period FY 2024/2025. Table 2.3 summarises the sector's exchequer issues in the first three months of FY 2025/2026.

Source:

National Treasury

Th e Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector received the highest proportion of exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 31 per cent, which is attributed to high proportions of exchequer transfers to the State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs and the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action at 36 per cent and 37 per cent, respectively.

[2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution]

Article 223 of the Constitution allows the national government to access additional funding during the budget implementation by spending money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose

under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need for unbudgeted expenditure arises for which no amount has been appropriated, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund.

Th e total approved additional funding by the Cabinet Secretary Th e National Treasury amounts to Kshs.43.50 billion, comprising Kshs.33.54 billion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.9.95 billion for development expenditure representing 1 per cent of the gross national budget. Th is was within the Constitutional threshold of ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament in any particular financial year (Kshs.4.69 trillion for FY 2025/26) in line with Article 223(5) of the Constitution.

In the first three months of FY 2025/2026 exchequer issues pursuant to Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya was Kshs.200 million, for recurrent expenditure, compared to Kshs.181.08 million), issued in a similar period of FY 2024/2025.

Table 2.10 shows exchequer issues under Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya during the reporting period.

Source:

In the first three months of FY 2025/2026, the Controller of Budget authorised a total of Kshs.200 million under Article 223 of the Constitution. Th e affected additional funding is to be regularised during the Supplementary I budget estimates.

[2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund]

Th e Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund to provide only essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.

In  the  first  three  months  of  FY  2025/26,  the  Controller  of  Budget  authorised  three  requests  amounting  to Kshs.116.16 million from the Equalization Fund. Th e amount comprised of, Kshs.68.16 million for Policy 1 development Trade Payables (Pending Bills) in favour of the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Kshs.48 million for the Second Policy development projects in Samburu County.

[3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget]

Th e approved gross national government budget for FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.4.69 trillion, representing 7 per cent growth compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion in FY 2024/2025. Th is comprised of Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.1.80 trillion for ministerial recurrent expenditures, and Kshs.2.14 trillion for CFS.  Ministerial development expenditure is to be funded through the net supply (from the government exchequer) of Kshs.407.10 billion and Appropriation-in-Aid (AIA) Kshs.337.74 billion.  Ministerial recurrent expenditure is to be funded by the government through the exchequer, amounting to Kshs.1,470.45 billion and AIA of Kshs.334.26 billion.   In FY 2025/26, the Equitable shareable revenue to County governments amounted to Kshs.415 billion.

To finance the budget, the government targeted to raise funds from various sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue  (Kshs.2.63  trillion),  Non-Tax  Revenue  (Kshs.127.65  billion),  Domestic  borrowing  (Kshs.1.10  trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.569.81 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.

[3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility]

Th e overdra ft facility is a way of short-term borrowing by the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months.  Kenya's Government overdra ft is administered through the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK).  It is restricted to a maximum of five percent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.

In the period under review, the overdra ft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged at an average interest rate of 9.6 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month.  In the first three months of FY 2025/2026, the total charge on the overdra ft facility was Kshs.697.47 million, as shown in Table 3.6.

Source:

National Treasury

Th e decline in overdra ft interest payments during the reporting period, compared to a similar period in FY 2024/25, was primarily due to the decrease in CBK's interest rates, which stood at 9.5 per cent in August 2025 compared to 12.75 per cent in August 2024.

[4.1.   Introduction]

MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. Th e chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first three months of FY 2025/2026. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. Th e chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first three months of FY 2025/2026.

Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.

In FY 2025/2026, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.703.07 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.58.16 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.

[4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector 4.2.1  Introduction]

Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. Th e ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Agriculture; and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.

Th e Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy, among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2025/26-2027/28, the sector plans to implement programmes that facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and the utilisation of the blue economy.

[4.3.1  Introduction]

Th e  Education  Sector  comprises  five  MDAs: Th e  State  Department  for  Vocational  and  Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education, the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research, the State Department for Basic Education and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.

Th e Sector envisions attaining ' Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development ' in Kenya. Th e Sector's strategic objectives include enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development capacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.

It is worth noting that the ongoing transition from the 8-4-4 to the 2-6-3-3 system requires substantial infrastructure, equipment, and human capital in the medium term, from 2025/26 to 2027/28.

[4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction]

Th is Sector consists of nine MDAs: Th e State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communications Technology and Digital Economy, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Energy, and Petroleum.

Th e EIICT sector aims to provide sustainable infrastructure development, a vibrant shipping and maritime industry, universal access to Information Communications Technology (ICT), Transport and built environment services, and accessible, affordable, quality and competitive energy and petroleum products.

text:
[4.5.1  Introduction]

Th e Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment and Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. Th e sector has several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, it has the following entities: Th e National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.

Th e goal of the Sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and low carbon emission, improving utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources. Th e Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country.

[4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector]

[4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector 4.6.1  Introduction]

Th e General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of eight MDAs, namely the State Departments for Trade; Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development; Cooperatives; Industry; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development; Investment Promotion; East African Community; and Tourism together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.

Th e objectives of the Sector over the MTEF period are to transform Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promote and sustain tourism, promote industrial development investments, enhance trade and ease of doing business, promote growth and development of cooperatives and the MSMEs Sector, promote regional integration, and promote equitable and sustainable ASAL and regional development.

[4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction]

Th e Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency

(WPA); the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNHCR); the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) and the State Department for Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs, as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.

Th e  Sector  creates  a  conducive  environment for the country's economic, social, and political development, which is necessary for fulfilling the objectives of Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption, public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.

It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption, public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.

Th is Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.

[4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector]

Th e budget allocation to GJLO in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.283.04 billion, compared to Kshs.230.89 billion allocated in the financial year 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 6 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 11 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.18.92 billion (7 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.264.12 billion (93 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e  State  Department for National Police Service received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.127.09 billion (50 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.530.33 million (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO Sector allocation).

Th e high allocation to the State Department for the National Police Service was due to the provision of security to the government's critical infrastructure and other related activities. Figure 4.11 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the GJLO Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/26.

Source: National Treasury

Th is amount comprised Kshs.3.77 billion for development expenditure, representing 42 per cent of development net estimates, and Kshs.62.69 billion for recurrent activities, representing 24 per cent of recurrent net estimates.

[4.8.1  Introduction]

Health is primarily a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. Th e health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. Th e sector comprises two MDAs: Th e State Department for

Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. Th e Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.

Th e Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles with a multi-sectoral approach as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). Th e Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.

[4.10.1  Introduction]

Th e Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely

Th e Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State Department for National Government Coordination, State Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State Department for Special Programmes; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; Th e National Treasury; State Department for Public Investments and Assets Management; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; Th e Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; Th e Auditor General; Th e Controller of Budget and Th e Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.

Th e  Sector  provides  national  leadership,  oversight,  and  policy  direction  towards  realising  the  country's  development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.

Th e  sector  has  prioritised  programmes  and  projects  aligned  with  the  Post-COVID-19  Economic  Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.

National Treasury

Th e total expenditure for the PAIR Sector amounted to Kshs.62.60 billion, representing 20 per cent of the gross estimates, compared to Kshs.55.99 billion (17 per cent) recorded   in the first three months of FY 2024/2025. Th is amount comprised Kshs.19.73 billion for the development budget representing an absorption rate of 16 per cent, compared to 18 per cent (Kshs.20.29 billion) recorded in the first three months of FY 2024/2025, and Kshs.42.87 billion for recurrent expenditure representing 22 per cent of the recurrent gross estimates, compared to 17 per cent (Kshs.35.71) recorded in a similar period of FY 2024/2025. Table 4.161 shows an analysis of exchequer issues and expenditure in the first three months of FY 2025/2026 for the PAIR Sector.

MDAs and National Treasury

Th e Executive Office of the President recorded the highest absorption of development budget at 36 per cent, while the State Department for Devolution recorded the lowest percentage of development expenditure to gross development estimates at 1 per cent. Conversely, the State House recorded the highest recurrent expenditure to gross estimates at 59 per cent, while the State Department for Special Programme recorded the lowest absorption of recurrent budget at 3 per cent.

[4.11.1  Introduction]

Th e Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises seven MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, Sports, Children Welfare Services, Culture, Th e Arts and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.

Th e strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.

text:
[4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector]

Th e budget allocation to SPCR in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.78.99 billion, compared to Kshs.83.93 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 2 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.24.85 billion (31 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.54.15 billion (69 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budget-

ary allocation of Kshs.29.32 billion (37 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.59 billion (5 per cent of the SPCR Sector allocation). Figure 4.19 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the SPCR Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/2026.

Source: National Treasury

[5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS]

In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed for seamless budget implementation. Th ese included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to an accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes, and Public debt management, as discussed below.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs]

Th e Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPS) is an end-to-end system that incorporates all procurement processes in line with the Public Procurements and Asset Disposal Act 2015 and its attendant Regulations to be used by all public procuring entities. Th e Implementation of the e-GP system is being carried out in a phased, incremental approach.

Phase I modules include: Registration (Supplier and Procuring Entity), Annual Procurement and Disposal Plan,  e-requisition,  e-tender  preparation,  e-tender  submission  &  evaluation,  e-tender  award,  e-framework agreement, e-bid security and guarantee management module, e-contract management, and e-Procurement Management Information System, as well as Workflow management. Phase II modules include e-Complaints, e-Compliance, e-Appeals, e-Debarment, Performance Management, Store Management, e-Auctions, e-Catalogues & Marketplace, and e-Reverse Auction.
heading_path: 5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[Observations]

Th e Public Procurement Regulatory Authority issued Circular No.04 2025 Ref: PPRA/6/5 Vol. II(229) dated 12th August 2025 on Enforcement of compliance with the Mandatory use of the Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPS) by all public procuring entities. Public entities were expected, effective 1st July 2025, to undertake all public procurement and asset disposal transactions through E-GPS.

Analysis of submitted financial and non-financial budget performance reports for the first three months of FY 2025/26 shows that requisition processes through the E-GPS were ongoing, resulting in low budget absorption of funds. Th e e-GPS has posed challenges to the procurement process due to a steep learning curve, integration issues with internal systems, and vendor-related problems that impact efficiency, competitiveness, and timely service delivery.

Recommendation: Accounting  Officers  should  fast-track  the  implementation  of  E-GPS  as  per  the  Circular  by PPRA and in compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act and directives issued by the National Treasury. Th is will enhance transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources.
heading_path: Observations
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting]

Pursuant to the Cabinet approval on 7th March 2024, government entities were to transition from a cash basis to an accrual basis, as subsequently gazetted vide Gazette Notice No. 11033 on 30th August 2024. MDAs adopted a 3-year phased approach to transition, with the first year being 2024/25.

MDAs have established committees to spearhead the transition, revised existing accounting policies and manuals, and conducted training for accountants, internal auditors, finance officers, and procurement officers. Th e first transitional statements were prepared and submitted to the Office of the Auditor General by 30th August 2025.
heading_path: 5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[Observations:]

Some of the Challenges highlighted by MDAs include: IFMIS is not configured to record accrual transactions and budget execution reported on cash basis even under the accrual reporting framework, entities budgets are prepared and executed on cash basis but FS are prepared on accrual basis thus requiring many reconciliations, Historical assets have not been valued, Challenges in determining fair value of donated assets such as motor vehicles, recognising the fair value of assets.

Recommendations: For the effective transition and implementation of a Cash to Accrual basis of Accounting, the Controller of Budget recommends continuous training of personnel in IPSAS-compliant recognition and measurement principles, upgrading financial systems to support accrual accounting, and conducting comprehensive asset verification and valuation exercises.

text:
[5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution]

Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya provides for Supplementary appropriation for the national government to spend money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need has arisen for expenditure for a purpose for which no amount has been appropriated by that Act, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund. Th e approval of Parliament for any spending under this Article shall be sought within two months a ft er the first withdrawal of the money, subject to clause (3). Clause 5 specifies that in any particular financial year, the national government may not spend under this Article more than ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that financial year unless, in special circumstances, Parliament has approved a higher percentage.

In accordance with Regulation 40(3) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations 2015, the purpose for which approval is sought for supplementary budget shall be Unforeseen and unavoidable, in circumstances where no budget provision was made; or Unavoidable, in circumstances where there is an existing budgetary provision, which is, however, inadequate.

Regulation 40(4) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulation 2015 identifies expenditure that shall not be considered unforeseen and unavoidable. Th is includes expenditure that, although known when finalising the estimates for the original budget, could not be accommodated within allocations, tariff adjustments, and price increases.

Th is reliance on Article 223 to finance foreseeable expenditures contravenes Paragraph 40(4) of the PFM (National Government) Regulations, 2015, highlighting weaknesses in budget planning and the overall reliability of budgeting.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution]

Th is reliance on Article 223 to finance foreseeable expenditures contravenes Paragraph 40(4) of the PFM (National Government) Regulations, 2015, highlighting weaknesses in budget planning and the overall reliability of budgeting.

Recommendation: Th e Controller of Budget recommends adopting good planning, budget practices and sound expenditure management by prioritising all essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation. In addition, the CS-TNT should expedite the submission of necessary documentation to Parliament for approval within the stipulated two-month period to ensure compliance with constitutional requirements.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

text:
[5.4.  Public Debt Management]

Article 201 of the Constitution guides all aspects of the principles of public finance in the Republic of Kenya. Article 201 (C) stipulates that the burdens and benefits of the use of resources and public borrowing shall be shared equitably between present and future generations. Th is is further elaborated under Section 15 (c)(d) of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 412A, 15 (c) over the medium term, the national government's borrowings shall be used only for financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure; 15 (d) public debt and obligations shall be maintained at a sustainable level as approved by Parliament for the national government and the county assembly for county government.

In FY 2025/26, the national government budget amounts to Kshs.4.69 trillion, comprising Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development, Kshs.1.80 trillion for ministerial recurrent and Kshs.2.14 trillion for Consolidated Fund Services expenditure. Allocation to Public Debt amounts to Kshs. 1.90 trillion, representing 41 per cent of the total budget, which is the highest proportion of the annual budget. Ministerial development expenditure recorded 16 per cent of the budget. Debt servicing has reduced the resources available for current spending needs. A significant portion of the government's budget is allocated to debt servicing, leaving less money for other development expenditures. Nonetheless, we commend the government's effort to automate the exchequer process for the national government. Only public-debt-related exchequer processes are yet to be automated.

Recommendation: To enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns. Recurrent expenditure should be contained through expenditure rationalisation and stronger public financial management controls.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[5.4.  Public Debt Management]

Recommendation: To enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns. Recurrent expenditure should be contained through expenditure rationalisation and stronger public financial management controls.

Th e Controller of Budget also recommends full automation and integration of the public debt management system to enhance accuracy and timeliness in data production. All foreign currency-denominated debt is presently being processed manually through the exchequer, whereas other exchequers are automated.

Further, for effective management of Public Debt, the government should implement comprehensive audits of debt procurement, utilisation, and sustainability. Th is should include auditing the public debt stock, reconciling loan books, and associating loans with specific projects. Th ere should be regular reviews aimed at flagging unsustainable debts to enhance sustainability, transparency and accountability in public borrowing. Th e audit findings should guide future borrowing and repayment strategies and alignment with national development priorities.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Three Months of FY 2025-26 b.pdf

text:
[6. CONCLUSION]

Th e  National  Government  Budget  Implementation  Review  Report  is  published  in  accordance  with  Article 228(6) of the Constitution, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit a report on the implementation of budgets for national and county governments to each House of Parliament every four months. It provides an overview of financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first three months of FY 2025/26 by analysing receipts into the Consolidated Fund and expenditure against the annual target. It also highlights key issues encountered during the review period and recommends mechanisms for addressing them.

Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.1.03 trillion, representing 23 per cent of the annual target. Th e Controller of Budget approved withdrawals of Kshs.1.02 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 23 per cent of the annual net estimates. Ministries, Departments and Agencies received a Kshs.409.80 billion, representing 22 per cent of the annual net estimates, comprising Kshs.43.31 billion for ministerial development expenditure (11 per cent) and Kshs.366.49 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure. Consolidated Fund Services received Kshs.546.76 billion, and County Governments received Kshs.66.13 billion as an equitable share of revenues raised nationally, representing 26 per cent and 16 per cent of the annual net estimates, respectively.

Gross expenditure for the National Government was Kshs.1.11 trillion, recording an absorption rate of 24 per cent. Th is  comprised ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.132.65 billion (absorption rate of 18 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure at Kshs.433.89 billion (absorption rate of 24 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.545.48 billion (absorption rate of 25 per cent).

[6. CONCLUSION]

In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed for seamless budget implementation. Th ese included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to an accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes, and Public debt management.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends that Accounting Officers should fast-track the implementation of E-GPS as per the Circular by PPRA and in compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act and directives issued by the National Treasury. Th is will enhance transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources and the absorption of the development budget. For the effective transition and implementation of a Cash to Accrual basis of Accounting, the Controller of Budget recommends continuous training of personnel in IPSAS-compliant recognition and measurement principles, as well as upgrading financial systems to support accrual accounting . To reduce over-reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution on foreseen expenses, it is necessary to adopt good planning and budget practices by prioritising all essential services and aligning them to operational realities during the budget process.   On public debt management, the Controller of Budget recommends that, to enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns, full automation and integration of the public debt management system to enhance accuracy and timeliness in data production and the government should implement comprehensive audits of debt procurement, utilisation, and sustainability
